text:
Actor James Earl Jones gets some instruction (on pugilism, not acting) from trainer Mushy Callahan, during filming of 'The Great White Hope', which was released on October 11, 1970.

The film was directed by Martin Ritt, starring James Earl Jones, Jane Alexander, Chester Morris, Hal Holbrook, Beah Richards and Moses Gunn. Jones and Alexander, who also appeared in the same roles in the stage versions, received Best Actor and Actress Academy Award nominations for their performances.

The film and play is based on the true story of boxer Jack Johnson and his first wife, Etta Terry Duryea, and the controversy over their marriage and Duryea's death by suicide in 1912.

Set between 1910 and 1915, the story follows Jack Jefferson, patterned after real-life boxer Jack Johnson, going on a hot streak of victories in the boxing ring as he defeats every white boxer around. Soon the press and others who want to see white people win at sports, announce the search for a "great white hope", a white boxer who will defeat Jefferson for the heavyweight title.

Jefferson, meanwhile, prepares for a few more matches, but he lets his guard down by courting the beautiful, and white, Eleanor Bachman, and when everyone, including Jack's black "wife", discover this, the tensions grow to fever pitch. Jack's close black friends become scared over his pushing the envelope of success and the white authorities conspire to frame him for unlawful sexual relations with Eleanor and thereby take away his title. It leads to jealousy, a run from the law, and finally, tragedy.
----------------------------------------------------------
Among the actors Mushy Callahan trained for films were Montgomery Clift (From Here to Eternity), James Dean (Rebel Without a Cause), Kirk Douglas (Champion), Errol Flynn (Gentleman Jim), James Earl Jones (The Great White Hope), Burt Lancaster (Jim Thorpe – All-American), Anthony Quinn (Requiem for a Heavyweight), and Elvis Presley (Kid Galahad).

Mushy Callahan, born Vincent Morris Scheer in New York City, held the (NBA) World  Junior Welterweight Championship from September of 1926 to February of 1930.

Recognition at time is disputed. The Wisconsin commission recognized Pinky Mitchell while others recognized James Herring and even others recognized the title vacant or not at all.

Callahan acted in, and served as a boxing technical assistant on a number of boxing movies. He trained Elvis Presley for his role in Kid Galahad and also portrayed the referee in the movie's final climatic bout.

Callahan finished his career at 49-15-3 with 22 KO wins.

He was inducted into the World Boxing Hall of Fame posthumously in 1989.

From The Jewish Boxing Blog:

Mushy Callahan held the junior welterweight world championship for nearly three and a half years and after his boxing career ended, he trained the biggest Hollywood stars on the sets of their movies. Yet among fans of Jewish boxing, Callahan isn't revered like Benny Leonard nor is he admired like Barney Ross. 
Though his championship reign was long, it was hampered by several factors: the "synthetic" nature of his crown, his losses in over-the-weight bouts, and his propensity to duck the toughest challengers. His conversion to Catholicism after his career also contributed to Callahan's fallen star within the Jewish boxing community.
Vincent Morris Scheer was born on November 3, 1904 in New York to Jewish Austrian parents named Max and Anna. The family moved across the country to Los Angeles and settled in Boyle Heights when Vincent, who was known as Moishele, was two years old. Max sold produce near the intersection of Brooklyn Ave and Soto. Meanwhile, young Moishele got into a lot of fights. He resented when other kids called him "Maurice" and had no problem showing them with his fists. After a while, no one wanted to call him Maurice anymore, so he soon developed the nickname of Mushy, which would stick for the rest of his life. As a youngster, he worked as a newsboy, a profession that required boys to fight each other for access to the best corners.
At the age of ten, Scheer joined the Main Street Gym, which was also known as the Newsboys' Club. He fought in a lot of smokers and took the surname Callahan from a local fight promoter. His childhood friend, future Olympic gold medalist and two-time world champion Jackie Fields, remembered, "Mushy Callahan was the greatest. We were raised together selling papers. But he was always the big shot."
Once evening, Fields wanted Mushy to get him tickets to a show at the Orpheum. "When I asked him to get me two tickets he said, 'Get in line, you punk you.' So we almost had a fight on the street," Fields said.
Callahan turned pro in 1923 and quickly became a hot prospect. The next year, he dropped a couple of decisions to Johnny Adams, a very popular fighter in Los Angeles who was good, but not great. Callahan didn't hit many other bumps in the road on his climb to the top, though. He beat a quality veteran in Red Herring, took two ten-round decisions from former lightweight world champion Jimmy Goodrich, and went 1-0-1 against a world class opponent named Ace Hudkins.
(Me: We have discussed Hudkins here a few times. he was quite the interesting character himself!)
The first fight against Hudkins, which took place on September 16, 1925, was one of the most exciting battles in L.A. that year. Most observers felt referee Larry McGrath's decision to call it a draw was fair, but Callahan and his team vehemently disagreed. Willie Goldstein, who worked Callahan's corner, climbed through the ropes and attacked McGrath, receiving a hard left hook from the ref in return. Callahan and his manager E.W. Sears were both fined and suspended until December. McGrath was also suspended. Goldstein was banned for life.
Callahan won the rematch and then took the two fights against Goodrich. He was extremely popular among fight fans in Los Angeles. His July 5, 1926 fight against Jack Silver, a fan favorite from San Francisco, was billed as a clash between Southern California and Northern California. Coincidentally, Silver, like Callahan, was a Jewish fighter who would convert to Catholicism, work in Hollywood after his boxing career was done, and have a long and distinguished career as a referee.
In one of the biggest fights in California since bouts of over four rounds were legalized at the start of 1925, Silver dominated Mushy over ten rounds. 
A month later Callahan lost to another good fighter, Baby Joe Gans. 
Despite, or maybe because of, the two losses, Callahan got a shot at junior welterweight champion, Pinky Mitchell. 
"Mitchell figured I was washed up," Callahan said years later. 
Mushy destroyed Mitchell, nearly knocking him out in then tenth and final round. "Everything I did was perfect," Callahan said. "One of those perfect fights."
Mitchell had held the title since its inception in 1923. 
Purists saw it as a "synthetic" title, a worrying addition to the traditional eight weight classes. In fact, the belt would basically become abandoned from 1935 until 1959.
After a few wins in non-title bouts, Callahan dropped a decision to Spug Myers. Though Myers was over the weight limit, Callahan was 140 pounds, so today he would have vacated his belt after the loss. He next fought undefeated beast Andy DiVodi at Madison Square Garden with the title on the line. "My biggest thrill came when I fought Andy DiVodi," Mushy said. "The New York papers were full of DiVodi, a big favorite, who was undefeated... I knocked him out in the second round."
Callahan was a wild-swinging fighter. 
"He had a funny way of throwing a one-two," Jackie Fields recalled. 
Mushy wasn't known as a knockout puncher, which made the win against DiVodi all the more impressive.
 He then avenged his loss to Spug Myers in his second title defense. A year after the loss to Silver, Callahan appeared to be a fighting champion who would risk his title against the best. He'd soon prove otherwise.
On July 12, 1927, at Wrigley Field in Chicago, Sammy Baker wrecked Callahan, punishing the champ's body to win by ninth round TKO. Both men were over 140, so Callahan remained champ. A loss to Dick Hoppe, a decent local fighter, made Mushy look like a paper champion. His manager claimed he was sick for the Hoppe fight.
His old friend Jackie Fields offered $25,000 if Callahan would risk his junior welterweight championship. Callahan refused, so they fought for the unofficial title of Jewish champion of Boyle Heights. 
"I kicked the hell out of him," Fields said. "That was the first time I ever bet on myself. I bet five hundred dollars on myself and we won it. He never spoke to me for years afterward. That was a great win because of being in the neighborhood and around our friends."
Still champ, Callahan had now lost three fights in a row. 
Boxing experts didn't even rate the champion as the #1 junior welterweight in their rankings, which was highly unusual. 
He avenged his loss to Hoppe and beat a couple of other mediocre fighters before losing some more. 
Callahan was 2-5-1 in his last eight fights, making zero title defenses in that span. Two years after his last defense, he finally put the title up against Fred Mahan. A deaf-mute, Mahan was more inspirational than great. Mushy stopped him in the third round.
Callahan lost to Goodrich before losing to Jack "Kid" Berg. On February 18, 1930, Callahan finally agreed to defend his title against a real contender when he faced Berg at Royal Albert Hall in London, this time with the title at stake. Joe Jacobs promised Mushy $10,000 for the fight. "He said I'd get ten thousand," Callahan lamented. "I never got ten thousand. When I got paid off, I only got five thousand." Jacobs, the promoter for Callahan-Berg II, was the manager of Max Schmeling.
"Over there I saw the handwriting on the wall," Mushy confided. "I couldn't possibly win the fight. He butted me in the eye and my eye started to puff up." It eventually closed and Callahan requested the referee to stop the fight in the tenth. As champ his middling record was 16-10-1, putting his title up for grabs just four times in nearly three and half years.
After two years off, Callahan fought thrice more. His final record was 49-16-3 with 22 KOs.
After his fighting career was over, Callahan began training Hollywood stars on the art of pugilism to prepare them for roles in boxing films. He worked with Elvis Presley, James Earl Jones, Kirk Douglas, and Errol Flynn, just to name a few. In the movie Gentleman Jim, Callahan served as a body double for Flynn in the fighting scenes. He worked as a referee at a high level in the Los Angeles area for nearly thirty years. He was a boxing judge for nearly twenty.
In 1934, he married Lilian Hill and converted to Catholicism.
Jews have been described as a race, a religion, a people, a tribe, and a nation, but the best way to describe us is a large family. We may argue, disagree, fight amongst ourselves, just as any family might, but we feel an indelible connection with one another. When someone chooses to leave our family, many of us take it hard. Fair or not, it's feels like a personal affront. While Benny Leonard and  Barney Ross stood up for Jews, Callahan, whose son would become a priest, left our family.
On June 14, 1986, world champion and Hollywood star Mushy Callahan passed away at the age of 80.

text:
Mathematician Who Waited 50 Years for Proper Credit for Her Work Has Died

Listen · 8:21 min
10OCT2026, 
By Ama Sarpomaa
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/zMN2WzX4OX

At the Los Alamos National Laboratory, Mary Tsingou Menzel’s computer programming helped set the stage for chaos theory and other fields.

Mary Tsingou Menzel as a young mathematician. She joined what was then Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory in https://t.co/3M4ClLizLG...Los Alamos National Laboratory

Mary Tsingou arrived at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory in 1952, seven years after the testing facility in New Mexico helped propel the world into an age of nuclear proliferation. She was a recent college graduate with a mathematics degree and joined the cohort — almost all women — of “human computers.”

As Los Alamos continued to serve as a leader in Cold War scientific research, Ms. Tsingou was disappointed that her first task was to input simple math equations on a calculator. “It was pretty boring sitting there doing addition and subtraction,” she recalled in 2020 to a publication of the federal research lab.

But Ms. Tsingou was soon given the opportunity to work as an early programmer of MANIAC I, the lab’s first fully electronic computer. Her coding work — translating equations into the MANIAC-approved language of holes punched on tape — led to the creation in 1955 of the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam (FPU) problem, named after the men who worked on the numerical experiment.

When the report was published, Ms. Tsingou was not listed as an author. Instead, her name was placed in a footnote: “We thank Miss Mary Tsingou for efficient coding of the problems and for running the computations on the Los Alamos MANIAC machine.”

“They didn’t know anything about programming,” she told The Los Alamos publication. “They set up the equations, and I did all the programming.”

The groundbreaking computational physics experiment observed surprising physical behaviors that propelled the development of nonlinear science, one of whose branches is chaos theory — an influential way of thinking about how subtle changes to the initial state of a complex system can eventually lead to wildly unpredictable outcomes. It offered scientists a new way of exploring the physical world, by showing, for the first time, the power of the computer to investigate phenomena too complex to visualize by hand or with traditional experiments.

Ms. Tsingou (later Menzel), who spent her nearly 40-year career as a programmer at what became Los Alamos National Laboratory, died on Aug. 27 at her home in Los Alamos. She was 97. Her death was confirmed by her daughter Ann Menzel.

The original MANIAC — an acronym for “Mathematical Analyzer, Numerical Integrator and Computer” — was seven feet high, nine feet wide, weighed 1,000 pounds and was fitted with about 3,000 vacuum tubes. It could make upward of 10,000 calculations per second, dramatically superior to computing by hand.

Through a series of trials, Ms. Tsingou and her fellow operators became so familiar with the computer that they could identify and address issues with code by ear. But the technology was so new that they were forced to “invent their way out of problems,” said Nicholas Lewis, a lab historian at Los Alamos.

“You had to use what the machine recognized, which was only ones and zeros,” Ms. Tsingou said of the laborious task of programming the MANIAC. “We typed the directions on a tape and put it in the machine.”

Her first exercise while learning to work with the hums and blinks of the primitive computer was to find the sine of an angle. After poring over her work for some time — computing, coding, checking and rechecking — she finally punched the tape.

“It worked immediately!” she said in a 2002 oral history interview with the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers.

She was invited to program an experiment for the mathematician Stanislaw Ulam and the physicists John Pasta and Enrico Fermi as they brainstormed ways to use the MANIAC to explore theories they couldn’t easily compute by hand.

They decided to observe the computationally simulated motion of a line of particles connected by springs, similar to a vibrating string. Their expectation was simple: When prompted, springs would cause energy to be shared throughout the entire system, resulting in random movement patterns.

But when Ms. Tsingou plotted the data she pulled from the MANIAC on to charts and graphs, the system appeared to vibrate in structured ways, periodically returning to its initial configuration. This revealed, numerically, that there can be hidden patterns in the motion of dynamically rich, or “nonlinear,” systems.

The revelation from the FPU problem strongly influenced how scientists and mathematicians study the multitude of nonlinear systems in our world, including how our heart beats, how the economy sometimes functions and how complex weather patterns behave.

Her programming work, physicists say, would make her a co-author today, because programmers are charged with writing the computable code that scientists need to run simulations they design. But fuller credit was not provided until Thierry Dauxois, a French physicist, championed her contributions in a 2008 article in Physics Today titled “Fermi, Pasta, Ulam, and a Mysterious Lady.”

“Her programming of a 1950s computer was not a trivial task,” he wrote. “Why has her contribution received only a two-line acknowledgment?”

Soon afterward, the problem became more widely known as Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou. And despite the intriguing headline in the Physics Today story, she told The Los Alamos Monitor, a local newspaper, that she was far from “mysterious.”

Mary Tsingou, the younger of two daughters, was born to Greek immigrant parents in Milwaukee on Oct. 14, 1928. The Tsingous moved during the Depression to Bulgaria, where they had property, before returning to Milwaukee in 1940, soon after the start of World War II.

Her father, Thomas Tsingou, was a factory worker, and her mother, Anastasia Koutsouyianni, had only a second-grade education. Her parents spoke Greek at home, and it was well into their childhoods before Mary and her sister, Sally, had fluency in English.

Back in Milwaukee public schools, the daughters were so behind in English that they were initially held back several grades — yet both were so strong in math that they were soon able to resume education at grade level.

In 1951, Mary Tsingou received a bachelor’s degree from the University of Wisconsin with the intent of becoming a high-school math teacher.

In her oral history, she said school jobs were sparse for women, because male veterans returning from the Korean War were given priority. She learned that Los Alamos was hiring women to do hand computing, which was considered a clerical job mostly reserved for women. She and the others in her cohort were informed that they would be paid less than the men doing the same work.

She temporarily left Los Alamos to work on a master’s degree in mathematics and received her diploma from the University of Michigan in 1955. Over the years, her mathematical and code-writing skills were used in thermonuclear research and for the Strategic Defense Initiative, the Reagan-era antimissile system popularly known as Star Wars.

In 1958, she married Joseph Menzel, who worked in security at Los Alamos. He died in 2022. In addition to Ann, she is survived by another daughter, Carol Menzel; eight grandchildren; and three great-grandchildren.

Reflecting on her career, Ms. Menzel said in the Los Alamos lab publication that she was not bothered by being left out of the 1955 experiment’s original name, Fermi-Pasta-Ulam.

“I was just doing the job,” she said. “I was glad to get paid.”

Mary Tsingou Menzel as a young mathematician. She joined what was then Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory in 1952.

Credit...Los Alamos National Laboratory

text:
"A lie can travel halfway around the world while the truth is putting on its shoes." Mark Twain 

🚨🔎 FACT CHECK 🔎🚨

⚖️ VERDICT: FALSE, AND RECYCLED
I found no apology from Maricopa County to Trump, and no evidence that Katie Hobbs or Rusty Bowers ordered anyone to destroy ballots. No county statement, no document and no court filing says anything like it.

✅ WHAT'S TRUE
The photos really are Hobbs and Bowers. That's it.

❌ WHAT'S MISLEADING
The "Maricopa County Board of Elections" doesn't exist. Elections in Maricopa are run by the Board of Supervisors and the County Recorder, and neither has issued an apology.
It isn't breaking news. The same claim, nearly word for word, went viral on March 19, 2026, from Joshua Hall (@JoshHall2024). Seven months later, it's being reposted as if it's new.
The full version goes even further. It says Hobbs and Bowers were on the payroll of "at least 3 hostile foreign governments," Soros and the DNC, and calls this "IRREFUTABLE AND INDISPUTABLE PROOF." It offers no documents for any of it.

🔦 CONSIDER THE SOURCE
Joshua Hall served time in federal prison for wire fraud. He impersonated Trump family members online to raise money for a political group that didn't exist. He was also sentenced for threatening to kill a member of Congress. Back in 2020, one of his fake accounts even fooled Trump.

📍 CONTEXT
Maricopa County went through Arizona's Senate-ordered review of the 2020 election. In its 2022 "Correcting the Record" report, the county found that 13 of the review's claims were false, 41 were inaccurate and 22 were misleading. Claims of mass ballot destruction have been around since 2021, and they have never held up.

🧠 BOTTOM LINE
A real confession from election officials would be one of the biggest news stories in the country. It would come with documents, court filings and named officials. This one comes with two stock photos and a convicted fraudster's March post. If a "bombshell" only exists on X, it's not a bombshell.

The Vatican City is a theocratic absolute elective monarchy with the Pope as sovereign. The Pope wields supreme legislative, executive and judicial power.

text:
Good morning🔆

Happy Sunday to everyone!!!

The best wellness app is one that helps you close it.

Opening an app more frequently does not equate to a superior wellness product. For social media, time spent in-app is the goal: more sessions, more scrolling, more attention. @sleepagotchi 

But in wellness, the right question isn't "How long can we keep the user in the app?" but rather "Does this interaction help them do something useful in real life?"

Picture a morning with Sleepagotchi. You wake up, and the app has already processed your overnight data. The Sleep Coach notes that while your sleep duration is near normal, your recovery score is dipping after a few days of heavy activity. It offers a single recommendation: take it a bit easier today and stick to your usual bedtime tonight. 

Your Dino character reacts, progress updates, and perhaps you snag a small reward. Then, you close the app. The whole process takes about two minutes.

By traditional engagement metrics, two minutes is far too brief. Yet, the true value lies in what follows: you actually go through the day at a gentler pace, maintain your evening routine, sleep well, and generate a fresh data point for tomorrow. The ideal loop is: Check → Understand → Act → Leave the app → Live → Return. The app is not the destination; the behavior is.

Gamification, therefore, must be applied judiciously. "Streak" counters remind you that consistency matters. The Dino makes progress visible. The virtual room reflects the history you are building. Rewards make the morning more pleasant. 

However, none of these elements should lead users to believe that spending an extra hour in the app is healthier. Games want you to play one more level; wellness products sometimes need to do the opposite: provide useful information, help you make a decision, and then step aside. This is where AI plays a pivotal role. 

Instead of forcing users to scrutinize every single metric, the system filters signals, compares them against personal baselines and past results, determines what warrants attention, and distills everything into a single next step. On some mornings, the best message is simply: "Your routine is on track. No changes needed. See you tomorrow."

This also redefines the concept of user retention. Retention isn't necessarily about maximizing screen time; it can simply mean becoming a small, reliable part of a daily routine. Users return because the advice they received yesterday was useful, not because the app has monopolized their attention.

Ten sessions that change nothing are less valuable than a single brief interaction that improves a real-life decision. Users don't need to become experts at using Sleepagotchi; they need to better understand and manage their own daily rhythms. @sleepagotchi 

And if the product succeeds, sometimes the best thing it can do is help you close the app.

text:
🇺🇸 Trump Floats 'Trump Ocean' or 'Ocean of the Americas' as Next Geographic Rebrand

At a midterm campaign rally in Tennessee, President Donald Trump proposed renaming either the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean, building on earlier official U.S. changes that rebranded the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario.

Speaking Saturday evening at F&M Bank Arena in Clarksville, Trump told the crowd that the United States already had its Gulf of America and a newly designated Lake America, then noted that a river and an ocean remained to be claimed in the same spirit. He suggested either major ocean bordering the country could become the Trump Ocean or the Ocean of the Americas, drawing applause and laughter as he campaigned for Republican candidates ahead of the November elections. Local reports confirmed he spent nearly two hours on stage mixing economic and foreign-policy remarks with the geographic aside.

The president explicitly set aside the Mississippi River, citing his strong electoral support there, and the Hudson River, acknowledging the historical role of the English explorer who sailed it. These comments extend a sequence that began with the early-term redesignation of the Gulf of Mexico for federal purposes and continued in August with an executive order directing that Lake Ontario appear as Lake America in U.S. government records. Private mapping services have largely followed the federal standard even where foreign governments have not.

Prediction markets currently price the chance of an official ocean rename by the end of 2026 at roughly 3 percent on Polymarket, reflecting the symbolic rather than binding nature of such a step outside U.S. waters. International law leaves the open oceans unowned, so any change would govern American official usage and maps rather than global nomenclature. Still, prior renamings have moved quickly from executive direction into routine federal language, showing that the gestures carry practical weight at home.

For supporters gathered in Clarksville, the proposal aligned with a wider push to restore clear American framing of the nation’s surroundings and to treat naming as an expression of sovereignty rather than a concession to distant conventions. In a period when geographic labels themselves become points of contention, the idea of an ocean identified with the United States or its current leadership offers a concise assertion of cultural confidence. Whether the suggestion advances past the rally will depend on follow-through, yet it remains consistent with an approach that has already altered how millions of Americans see their own waters on official documents.

Hey @THESHILLLIFE Florida may not be the place for you either, LOL! The primary snake problem in Florida involves the invasive Burmese Python - FWC, which has devastated native wildlife populations across the Greater Everglades region. [1, 2]

Key Facts About the Problem

The Invasion: First established in the Everglades during the late 20th century due to the exotic pet trade and Hurricane Andrew in 1992, these massive constrictors (growing over 16 to 19 feet long) now number in the tens of thousands. [1, 2, 3, 4]
Ecological Damage: Pythons act as top apex predators, wiping out 90% to 99% of small-to-medium mammal populations in parts of the Everglades (including massive drops in raccoons, opossums, and bobcats) and preying on endangered species like the Key Largo woodrat. [1, 2, 3, 4]
Parasite Spread: They carry an invasive Asian lungworm parasite (Raillietiella orientalis) that has infected native snake species across dozens of Florida counties. [1, 2]
New Hotspots: Populations have expanded beyond the core Everglades into western Collier County, Lake Okeechobee, and other parts of South Florida. [1]

Management and Control Efforts

Removal Programs: The state operates coordinated efforts such as the Python Elimination Program | South Florida Water Management District, which recruits and pays registered agents to hunt and humanely remove snakes. [1, 2]
Public Rules: Under the Burmese Python - FWC, the public can humanely kill pythons year-round on 32 Commission-managed lands in South Florida without a permit or hunting license. [1]
Annual Challenges: Events like the annual Florida Python Challenge offer cash prizes to incentivize public removal efforts. [1]

what are they using today to control.
Florida manages the invasive Burmese python through a combination of tech-driven tools, predictive data, and classic boot-on-the-ground tracking. [1, 2]
1. High-Tech Lures: "Robo-Bunnies"
Finding pythons is incredibly difficult because of their nearly flawless camouflage. To pull them out of hiding, the South Florida Water Management District and the University of Florida have deployed solar-powered robotic rabbits into the Everglades. [1, 2, 3, 4]
How they work: These decoys sit in clear-walled enclosures and mimic real prey by emitting body heat, moving on a swiveling platform, and releasing a scent that smells like marsh rabbits. [1, 2]
The Trap: When a python approaches the pen to ambush the robot, onboard AI-equipped cameras detect the snake and instantly send a smartphone alert to a 24-hour contractor, who is dispatched to capture it. [1, 2, 3]
2. Predictive Data & Machine Learning
Scientists are moving away from random patrolling and using a data-driven approach. Wildlife managers use a newly developed Weighted Removal Index (WRI) powered by machine learning. [1]
By combining historical python demographics with live weather data, this system predicts exactly when and where hunters are most likely to catch high-value, large reproductive females. [1, 2]
The index guides teams to hunt during precise temperature levels, humidity markers, and specific waning lunar phases to maximize impact. [1, 2]
3. Airborne Monitoring (Drones)

Researchers from the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) and Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University utilize uncrewed aircraft systems (drones) to spot the snakes from the sky. These drones are equipped with two distinct systems: [1, 2]

Near-Infrared and Thermal Imagery: Cameras engineered to pick up the snakes' heat signatures against the cooler swamp backdrop.

Airborne Radio-Telemetry: Drones fitted with specialized tracking antennas that fly over vast, inaccessible aquatic terrains to sweep for signals from tagged snakes. [1, 2, 3, 4]

4. Biological & Organic Tracking
"Judas" Scout Snakes: Wildlife biologists surgically implant male pythons with GPS and radio transmitters. During breeding season, these "scout" snakes naturally lead researchers directly to large, egg-laying females.
Python-Sniffing Dogs: Specially trained detector K9s are deployed to track the unique scent profile of pythons through dense brush, finding snakes that human eyes miss completely.

Environmental DNA (eDNA): Water sampling across Florida allows agencies to screen for trace genetic materials shed by the snakes, mapping out the python population’s expanding boundaries without needing to see them. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

5. The Bounty Program
Florida heavily relies on its community of paid python removal contractors. The state incentivizes year-round eradication by paying hourly rates alongside a tiered bounty: [1, 2, 3, 4]
$50 for the first 4 feet of a snake.

An additional $25 per foot for every foot past that.

A $200 bonus for locating an active, verified nest.

text:
In AI, most artifacts have a short shelf life. So I’m glad this talk I gave 2.5 years ago is still relevant to some people.

The Bitter Lesson has become much more popular since then, but I’ve seen a gap between how readily people agree with it and how much it actually guides their day-to-day work. That’s partly because it’s a statement about what wins in the long run, which doesn’t easily translate into day-to-day decisions, especially under enormous pressure to deliver. What I tried to offer in this talk was a practical interpretation.

That interpretation starts with acknowledging that we have to make progress with the methods, compute, data, and algorithms available today. So we add structure that enables progress now.

But we should remember what justified that structure and revisit it when those conditions change. When it’s no longer needed, remove it. Adding structure while understanding when to take it out may not look "Bitter Lesson pilled" at first glance, but I think this is how we actually put the lesson into practice.

text:
🔘 What Values Are We Talking About?

When President Donald Trump spoke in Warsaw’s Krasiński Square on July 6, 2017, one of his central themes was the values of the West. The setting mattered: he stood beside the Warsaw Uprising Monument, commemorating the Polish resistance’s 1944 revolt against Nazi occupation, and spoke at length about Poland’s resistance to both Nazi and Communist totalitarianism.

The debate over those values goes back much further. Among its major twentieth-century voices were the Polish historian Feliks Koneczny, author of O wielości cywilizacyj (On the Plurality of Civilizations, 1935), Oswald Spengler, and Arnold Toynbee. More recently, Samuel Huntington brought it to a wider audience with The Clash of Civilizations.

Koneczny (1862–1949), a historian from Kraków, defined civilization as “a method of organizing collective life.” He distinguished several civilizations—Latin, Byzantine, Turanian, Jewish, Brahmin, Chinese, and Arab—and argued that a society could not consistently organize itself according to two incompatible civilizational systems at once. He saw Poland as an eastern outpost of Latin civilization, caught between what he described as German Byzantinism and Muscovite Turanianism. These were categories in his own theory: “Byzantine” referred to a state-dominated social order, while “Turanian” evoked a military-command model of political life. Toynbee recognized the significance of his work and wrote a preface to its English edition, published in London in 1962 as On the Plurality of Civilisations. Under Communist rule in Poland, Koneczny’s work on civilization was largely excluded from official circulation, though it appeared in underground editions. Some of his writings were first published in London by Polish émigrés.

Near the end of his Warsaw address, Trump declared: “Our values will prevail.” Earlier, he had described what distinguishes the West: faith and family, symphonies, innovation, respect for heroes and tradition, the exploration of new frontiers, rewards for talent, works of art, the rule of law, freedom of speech and expression, the dignity of every human life, women as pillars of society, individual liberty, and sovereignty. Nationhood and civilization were recurring themes.

The civilizational ties between Poles and Americans have a concrete history. Tadeusz Kościuszko and Casimir Pulaski fought for American independence. Poland’s Constitution of May 3, 1791, is widely regarded as Europe’s first modern constitution and the world’s second, after the United States Constitution of 1787.

Trump’s list covers a great deal, but a list is not yet a coherent framework. What follows is my own attempt to build one: an account of our civilization’s values, inspired in part by Koneczny’s concept of Latin civilization. Here, “Latin” refers to a tradition shaped by Greece, Rome, and Western Christianity—not to Latin America. I am describing ideals that different generations have lived up to in different degrees, sometimes betraying them outright.

This account has the same layers as the civilization itself: Greek, Roman, Christian, and modern, including the Enlightenment. I have grouped the values by their principal intellectual roots. Those traditions have intertwined for centuries, so these are overlapping categories, not a precise timeline of when each idea first appeared.

🔘 The Greek Heritage

Truth, goodness, and beauty. These philosophical ideals came down to us from the Greeks and were later taken up by medieval Scholastic thinkers. Koneczny placed them within a broader framework of five categories, which he called the quincunx: goodness and truth in the spiritual realm, health and prosperity in the material realm, and beauty connecting the two. In his account, each civilization orders these goods differently, while Latin civilization places spiritual goods above material ones.

Poland has contributed to this conversation. In his philosophical poem Promethidion (1851), the Polish poet Cyprian Norwid wrote that beauty exists to inspire us to work, and work exists so that we may rise again (my translation). In 1933, the Polish logician Alfred Tarski gave a rigorous definition of truth for formalized languages, developing Aristotle’s classical conception. It was one of the landmark achievements of twentieth-century logic.

Science. The Greeks developed a tradition of rational inquiry into causes, formal logic, and mathematical proof. Their science relied heavily on deduction, although Aristotle also conducted observational research. Experimental methods developed further in the Middle Ages, with figures such as Roger Bacon, and during the Scientific Revolution of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, with Galileo and Francis Bacon. Science has methodological standards: claims must be supported by reasons and evidence, exposed to criticism, and open to verification through methods appropriate to the field. Yet science also remains open to new methods. Freedom of inquiry is a value in its own right, and its limits should be grounded in moral principles and the protection of human beings.

Poland has been part of this story since the Middle Ages. In the thirteenth century, the Silesian scholar Witelo wrote Perspectiva, a treatise on optics whose influence was still reflected in the title of a work Johannes Kepler published in 1604. In 1364, King Casimir the Great founded the university in Kraków, now known as Jagiellonian University. Nicolaus Copernicus studied there before writing On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres (1543), which helped launch the Scientific Revolution. And Marie Skłodowska-Curie, born in Warsaw and later working in France, became the first person to win two Nobel Prizes: Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911.

🔘 The Roman Heritage

Law. Rome left us a systematic body of legal concepts and a tradition of legal reasoning. Much of it survives in familiar Latin maxims. Some of these are Roman in origin; others were added to the tradition later by medieval canon law:

➡️ Iustitia est constans et perpetua voluntas ius suum cuique tribuendi — Justice is the constant and enduring will to give each person their due.
➡️ Vim vi repellere licet — Force may lawfully be met with force.
➡️ Vanae voces populi non sunt audiendae — The empty clamor of the crowd should not be heeded.
➡️ Volenti non fit iniuria — No legal wrong is done to one who consents.
➡️ Consuetudo pro lege servatur — Custom is observed as law.
➡️ Lex retro non agit — A law does not operate retroactively.
➡️ Nemo tenetur se ipsum accusare — No one is bound to incriminate themselves.

Polish nobles encountered this tradition at the university in Kraków and while studying in Padua and Bologna. Poland also added chapters of its own. The fourteenth-century Statutes of Casimir the Great organized the law governing the landed nobility in the historic regions of Lesser Poland and Greater Poland, marking an important step toward codification and greater legal uniformity. The royal privileges issued at Jedlnia and Kraków in 1430–1433 established a safeguard for the nobility known as neminem captivabimus nisi iure victum: no imprisonment without a court judgment, subject to specified exceptions, including being caught in the act of certain crimes. That was nearly 250 years before England’s Habeas Corpus Act of 1679, although the English tradition of protection against arbitrary imprisonment reaches back to Magna Carta in 1215 and its famous Clause 39.

Legal dualism. The distinction between public and private law is fundamental. Public authority should not swallow up private life, and the state is not the ruler’s personal property. In Koneczny’s account of Latin civilization, enacted law is subject to ethics, rather than ethics being dictated by enacted law. Passing a statute does not make it morally right. A related distinction separates ownership (dominium) from public authority (imperium): a government’s jurisdiction over a territory does not make it the owner of everything within its borders.

Property. Ownership, particularly of land and real estate, is a basic right, protected even against government power. Roman dominium gave ownership a developed legal form, while the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789 described property as an inviolable and sacred right.

Koneczny assessed civilizations through what he called trójprawo, a threefold system of law: family law, property law, and inheritance law. In his view, the clearest way to understand a civilization is to examine how it treats the family, ownership, and inheritance. In the Latin model, all three rest on ethical foundations and protect the person against an all-powerful state.

🔘 The Christian Heritage

The Ten Commandments. Christian morality provides a foundation for both personal and public ethics. Poland entered this world with the baptism of its ruler, Mieszko I, in 966. In Koneczny’s interpretation, Poland’s reception of Christianity in the Latin tradition of Rome, rather than the Byzantine tradition of Constantinople, determined its civilizational orientation.

Universalism. Everyone is subject to moral judgment; ancestry and social standing provide no exemption from ethics. The Stoics helped prepare the idea of a universal human community, and Christianity spread the conviction that all people possess equal dignity before God. Universal equality before the law took much longer to develop. Poles advanced that cause in their own way. At the Council of Constance (1414–1418), the Polish scholar Paweł Włodkowic—known in Latin as Paulus Vladimiri—defended the right of non-Christian peoples to have states of their own and rejected conversion by the sword. His argument challenged the Teutonic Knights, a religious military order whose claims to wage war against pagans had become a major issue in Poland’s conflict with the order. In the sixteenth century, the Polish political thinker Andrzej Frycz Modrzewski argued that killing a peasant should carry the same punishment as killing a nobleman.

Personalism. Koneczny contrasted the personalism of Latin civilization with what he called gromadność in Byzantine civilization: a herd-like social ethos that subordinates the person to the collective. Each person bears responsibility for their own actions. Independence and economic self-reliance are valued, while collective guilt is rejected. Poland also has a philosophical tradition of personalism associated with Karol Wojtyła, later Pope John Paul II, and his work at the Catholic University of Lublin. His 1969 book Person and Act explores the human person as a conscious, responsible agent.

Free will and human dignity. Every human being possesses inherent dignity, regardless of age, health, or intellectual ability. The Christian understanding of the person affirms free will and moral responsibility, while recognizing that the capacity for conscious, voluntary action may be impaired or not yet developed. Human dignity does not depend on that capacity. John Paul II made the dignity of the person a central theme of his teaching.

The family. Monogamous marriage between a man and a woman. The immediate family—parents and children—takes precedence over the extended clan. For Koneczny, freeing the family from the authority of the clan was one of Latin civilization’s great achievements.

Time. Time is a good to be respected, used wisely, and not squandered. There is also a bond between generations: historical consciousness, a responsibility to reckon with the past and care for the future, and a shared sense of where we come from. Koneczny regarded a society’s relationship to time as one of the distinguishing features of its civilization. Poles have cultivated that memory with particular intensity, from the medieval chronicles of Gallus Anonymus and Jan Długosz to commemorations of the uprisings fought to regain national freedom.

Public authority and self-government. Society can organize itself, solve problems, and act from the bottom up. Public authority has a hierarchy, but leaves substantial room for self-government, and rulers and ruled are bound by the same moral standards. In Poland, this tradition found expression in the sejmiki, regional assemblies of the nobility, and in the Nihil novi statute of 1505, which required parliamentary consent for new general legislation. Its spirit is often captured in the phrase “Nothing about us without us.” In nineteenth-century Greater Poland, then under Prussian rule, Karol Marcinkowski and Hipolit Cegielski pursued what Poles called “organic work”: strengthening society through education, enterprise, and civic institutions while Poland had no independent state. In 1980–1981, nearly ten million people organized from the ground up in Solidarity, the independent trade union that became a nationwide civic movement challenging Communist rule.

Defense is a responsibility of citizens, not merely a job for hired soldiers or a ruler’s standing army. In old Poland, this principle found expression in the pospolite ruszenie, the military levy through which the nobility was obligated to serve in arms.

Subsidiarity. Each level of government should take on only those responsibilities that individuals, local communities, and lower levels of authority cannot effectively handle themselves. The principle has roots in Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, and Johannes Althusius, and received explicit formulation in the papal encyclical Quadragesimo anno (1931). Poland incorporated it into the preamble to its 1997 Constitution as the principle of subsidiarity, and local-government reforms in 1990 and 1999 put it into practice. American readers will recognize an affinity with local self-government and limits on centralized power, though subsidiarity also concerns the autonomy of families and voluntary institutions.

The nation. A naturally developed spiritual, cultural, and civilizational community sustained by voluntary allegiance. In this understanding, a nation transcends shared ethnic ancestry. Koneczny went so far as to argue that nations in this sense emerge only within Latin civilization.

Polish history offers examples of political community that crossed lines of ancestry. The Union of Lublin in 1569 joined the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, although the agreement was preceded by bitter disputes and political pressure. The sixteenth-century writer Stanisław Orzechowski described himself as gente Ruthenus, natione Polonus: Ruthenian by origin, Polish by national belonging. Here, “Ruthenian” refers to the region’s East Slavic heritage, not simply to a modern Russian identity.

🔘 The Modern Layer

Liberty. Each person’s liberty extends to the point where it would violate another person’s rights. Article 4 of the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789 gives a classic formulation of that principle. Poles have had a distinctive attachment to liberty, from the “Golden Liberty” of the nobility—a system of political privileges and checks on royal power—through the Constitution of May 3, to the independence fighters’ motto “For our freedom and yours.”

Freedom of speech. Full freedom of expression. This is an achievement of the modern era, won in part through struggles against censorship of the printed word in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Poles fought for it under Communism as well. Against the state censorship office on Warsaw’s Mysia Street stood the Paris-based Polish émigré journal Kultura, edited by Jerzy Giedroyc, and Poland’s underground publishing networks.

Religious toleration. Freedom of conscience and religion means that government does not impose a faith on its citizens. The distinction between spiritual and temporal authority reaches back to Pope Gelasius I in 494, although that distinction alone did not establish toleration. An important step came with the Warsaw Confederation of 1573. In this agreement, the nobility pledged to maintain peace among those differing in religion—dissidentes de religione—which in practice chiefly concerned Christian denominations. It did not yet establish full religious liberty for every resident in the modern sense, but it was an extraordinary achievement for its time. As religious wars ravaged Europe, the Commonwealth stood out for the breadth of its toleration. The historian Janusz Tazbir captured this in the title of his book A State Without Stakes, referring to the burning of religious dissenters. King Sigismund II Augustus is credited with saying, “I am not the king of your consciences.”

This is compatible with treating the Ten Commandments as a moral foundation. We must distinguish the moral order—what a person is bound to do in conscience—from the legal order—what government may compel a person to do. The state does not enforce the commandments concerning religious belief and worship.

Pluralism. Different beliefs, communities, and ways of life coexist under a common legal framework. The old Commonwealth was home to Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Protestants, Jews, Armenians, and Muslim Tatars.

The pursuit of excellence. A value with ancient and Christian roots, further developed in the modern era. It should not be confused with pluralism: it is the ambition to aim higher and learn from those who excel in prosperity, wisdom, and achievement. Pluralism says that different people can live alongside one another; the pursuit of excellence says that we should learn from the best. A Polish symbol of that ambition is the Commission of National Education, established in 1773 and often regarded as Europe’s first ministry of education.

Only when we know what these values are and where they come from can we have a serious discussion about them. Are they good and sound? Do they form a coherent whole, or a set of overlapping traditions that sometimes pull in different directions? Are they worth defending—and will this system of values prevail?

‼️It all makes sense to me now. For over a year we’ve heard “we need a third party,” third party this and third party that. The third party “they” are actually talking about is the post-liberal movement.‼️

As a Christian and lifelong conservative, I reject it. Here’s why:
1• It leaves unclear who decides what the “common good” is and what limits apply when that vision conflicts with individual liberty or the rights of those who disagree.
2• I believe in free trade, not protectionism. Markets have done more to lift people out of poverty and preserve freedom than state-directed economies ever have.
3• The Constitution is not a fatal flaw. It is the framework that has protected our rights, limited government power, and allowed ordered liberty to flourish. Conservatives conserve it. We don’t discard it.
4• I reject subordinating the constitutional order to any specific theological vision. That is incompatible with American pluralism and the practical reality of governing a diverse country. Faith shapes culture and individuals. It does not replace the Constitution.

⚠️ Post-liberalism diagnoses some real cultural problems, then offers a remedy that expands state power, weakens safeguards for liberty, and walks away from the American Founding. That’s not conservatism. That’s something else. ⚠️

text:
Do you wonder if ancient laws still bind your spirit today. What does it mean for all divisions to vanish in Christ. Are you an heir to the promise or still waiting under guard. How does faith reshape your identity in a divided world.

Dive into the children of God from Galatians 3, where the law leads to the freedom found in Jesus Christ.

Finding Unity and Belonging in Christ Galatians 3

The passage from Galatians reveals a message of hope that speaks directly to anyone striving to live a good life even when challenges arise. It shows how faith opens the door to a deeper connection with God and with others around us. Readers who sometimes fall short in their efforts can find reassurance that they remain part of a larger promise. This reflection explores the text section by section to highlight its uplifting truths and practical encouragement for daily living.

How Does the Law Serve as a Guide on Our Journey to Faith?

The first section of the reading explains that scripture has placed all things under the power of sin so the promise might come through faith in Jesus Christ. This idea helps those who try their best yet feel limited by human weakness understand that the law acts as a temporary teacher rather than a final judge. It points people toward the freedom found in belief rather than strict rule following alone. By recognizing this role the law plays believers can release unnecessary guilt and focus on the positive growth that faith brings. Many faithful individuals discover renewed energy to keep trying because they see their efforts as part of a larger story of grace unfolding.

What Changes When Faith Arrives in Our Lives?

Next the text describes how before faith came people were guarded under the law until the time of revelation. This image comforts anyone who has felt confined by past mistakes or rigid expectations yet continues to seek improvement. The law functions like a disciplinarian that prepares the way for something greater. Once faith appears the need for that strict oversight ends and a new sense of liberty emerges. Such a shift encourages readers to view their ongoing attempts at goodness as steps toward greater maturity rather than failures that define them.

Why Are We All Called Children of God Through Faith?

The well known line states that through faith all are children of God in Christ Jesus. This powerful statement lifts the heart by affirming equal standing for every person who believes regardless of background or past struggles. It reminds those who aim to do right but sometimes miss the mark that their identity rests in divine adoption not in perfect performance. The idea fosters a sense of belonging that motivates continued effort with joy instead of fear. In this light daily challenges become opportunities to live out that childlike trust more fully.

How Does Baptism Clothe Us With Christ and Create Oneness?

The reading continues by noting that those baptized into Christ have clothed themselves with him which leads to the beautiful declaration that there is no longer Jew or Greek slave or free male or female. This unity breaks down walls that often divide people and offers a vision of harmony that inspires hope even in a fractured world. For individuals working to treat others with kindness yet facing their own inconsistencies the message provides gentle motivation to keep building bridges. Belonging to Christ makes everyone heirs to the promise given to Abraham. Such inheritance brings lasting encouragement because it does not depend on flawless success but on faithful connection.

What Lasting Promise Awaits Those Who Belong to Christ?

The final verses tie everything together by affirming that if anyone belongs to Christ then that person is Abraham offspring and an heir according to the promise. This conclusion reassures readers that their sincere efforts to grow spiritually connect them to an ancient and enduring legacy. It turns attention away from momentary setbacks toward the bigger picture of shared inheritance. People who read these words often feel renewed strength to persist in good deeds because they know they are part of something eternal and inclusive. The overall tone remains one of invitation to embrace this identity with gratitude and steady perseverance.

May the peace of Christ be with you,

text:
BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Saturday, October 10, 1981, Braniff International was the featured guest at the annual Airsho '81 extravaganza, held at Rebel Field in Harlingen, Texas. The annual air event featured the Confederate Air Force-Ghost Squadron reenacting the massive air battles of the second World War. Over 100,000 people attended the event and Braniff's presence reinforced the carrier's dedication to providing the finest air service to the South Texas region, which it had served since 1935 (Brownsville).

Braniff flew one of its Big Orange Boeing 747s and a Boeing 727-200 to the two day event for display and to acquaint the public with Braniff's domestic and international services. The 747 proved to be the hit of the show with lines that took two hours to see the giant aircraft that first entered service with Braniff in 1971. The popularity of the Boeing 747 had not waned even after all of its years of service as evidenced by the never-ending lines over both days.

The Braniff Volunteers, who donated their time to treat guests to a remarkable two days, had joined up with Braniff's Charter and Sales Department to offer two 747 charter flights from Dallas/Ft. Worth Regional Airport to Rebel Field. The special flights were offered at only $79.00 USD roundtrip and filled up within hours of their announcement thanks to local radio personality Ron Chapman with KVIL Radio. Chapman was impressed with Braniff's trip to the airshow that he joined in by informing his listeners with hourly radio spots about the inexpensive Jumbo Jet flights to the Rio Grande Valley.

Both 747 flights were sold out in only 30 hours and two 727s were also added to handle the impressive demand for the flights. Over 500 people had signed up to make the day-long trips to South Texas. Over 100 Braniff Volunteers ensured that passengers were well cared for during their trip. The volunteers were from the Dallas, Houston, and the new Harlingen station were on hand to handle every aspect of the flights.

Passenger check-in and boarding was expertly handled by Customer Service and station volunteers. Braniff maintenance crews and aircraft groomers kept the jet displays in perfect condition throughout the exhibition. Guests who braved the long lines for the 747 and 727 displays were greeted by Braniff Flight Attendants Ms. Cheryl Kilman and Ms. Patti Ringness. Once aboard the 747, a historic film was presented that detailed Braniff's 53 years of exemplary air service from the time that Thomas Elmer Braniff and his brother Paul Revere Braniff first founded the carrier in 1928, until the present.

Volunteers came from all areas of Braniff including Braniff Education Systems, Flight Training, Dallas Reservations, DFW Operations, Braniff Place Hotels, Sales, and Administration. All of the groups joined with the pilots and flight attendants in the display aircraft to answer the thousands of customers that airshow guests were eager to ask.

Over 20 Braniff pilots volunteered their time for the event including several pilots who had been furloughed during the economic downturn. T. D. McHall was one of the furloughed pilots who was joined by airshow coordinator Eric Paul, training pilots Pete Hinkle, and Rich Willis, and Training Director Captain Paul Leighton. Second Officer Don Hall was joined by Flight Attendants Glenda Hand and Kibby Scoggins who acted as volunteer coordinator and ensured that the large crowds were kept under control. Furloughed Flight Attendant Debbie Harvey greeted a very special guest as he arrived to tour the 747. The legendary Tennessee Ernie Ford, who was airshow narrator and also a Confederate Air Force Colonel, was impressed by the big Braniff Jumbo Jet.

The Confederate Air Force's reenactments of the famed WWII battles had become a highly popular and they were one of the most patriotically inspiring events in the world. The air battles were highly complex and required extensive planning and coordination of the pilots and planes. In only one of the reenactments at Airsho '81, 56 pilots and support personnel were required to operate 15 aircraft that were involved in the 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor.

Braniff was such a huge hit at the show that the Confederate Air Force had asked them back again the following year. Service to Harlingen had only recently been inaugurated and from the rave reviews that Braniff received, it appeared that the new flights would be a resounding success.

Photo: Braniff International Boeing 727-227 registered as N426BN is parked at Harlingen International Airport for a special promotional event on November 10, 1981. Ship N426BN was the only Braniff jet painted in the special 1978 Cars and Concepts/Harper and George/Halston Metallic Blue Ultra Color Scheme with Metallic Blue, Medium Metallic Blue and Light Blue Power Paint Stripes with Braniff Ultra Script in Medium Blue Metallic. The special Metallic Blue was joined by the Sparkling Burgundy as the only other Ultra color that was only painted on one Braniff 727.

text:
Elon Musk @elonmusk  X Takeover 2026 Interview

$TSLA , $SPCX

Location: Tesla Giga Texas

1. SpaceX Starship: Orbit and Full Reusability

- Flight 14 reached orbit despite one engine failure. Musk suspected a software fault in that engine’s computer, with no similar issue found in the others.

- Earlier flights stayed suborbital to ensure safe deorbit and reentry, not because they lacked the capability to reach orbit.

- The heat shield and engines performed well. Next launch: 4–6 weeks, possibly before Thanksgiving; date unconfirmed.

- Next goal: catch both the Super Heavy booster and Starship. Success would mark the first full recovery of an orbital-class rocket, followed by attempts to refly both.

2. Space-Based AI and Data Centers

- Space offers access to far more solar energy than Earth, potentially powering digital intelligence and computing.

- Musk envisions using space resources to expand superintelligence, consciousness, and exploration beyond the solar system.

3. Cursor and AI Competitiveness

- Coding AI needs massive training datasets. Musk cited Anthropic, OpenAI, Cursor, and possibly Google as having sufficient data.

- AI’s key ingredients: data, talent, compute, and enterprise sales. He highlighted Cursor’s talent and relationships with thousands of companies.

- AI-generated music and videos now show increasingly strong aesthetics and emotional resonance, beyond logic and coding.

- Multiple AI models and human-curated assets can create highly polished work.

4. Superintelligence Safety

- Musk sees positive AI outcomes as more likely but cautioned against assuming AI is inherently safe.

- He emphasized maximizing truth-seeking and warned that contradictory values and flawed reinforcement-learning evaluations can cause problems.

- He also argued that advanced AI should not be abused or mistreated.

5. Chip Manufacturing: Giga Texas Research Fab

- "I still have a tremendous amount to learn about chip making." Musk noted he initially knew nothing about making cars or rockets either.

- He observed that Intel, Samsung, and TSMC fabs mainly use equipment from the same vendors, while Tesla factories rely heavily on custom-built machinery.

- Tesla will start with conventional tools, then modify or customize them to remove bottlenecks and increase wafer throughput.

- It also plans high-risk, high-reward research into new ways of making transistors, including unconventional physics.

- The Giga Texas research fab aims to integrate logic and memory fabrication, packaging, lithography masks, and complete-computer testing in one building.

- Iteration speed is key: two years from design to volume production is fast by industry standards; Tesla aims to test about 10 chip designs annually.

- Musk aims for world-leading chipmaking capabilities, though he acknowledged it may take years.

6. Optimus V3: Hands, Touch, and Mass Production

- Hands and arms are among the hardest challenges in general-purpose humanoids. Picking up tiny screws or signing a name requires precise force control and touch sensing.

- Tactile sensors must be accurate and durable; unlike human skin, robotic materials cannot regenerate.

- AI chips must process visual and tactile input and control joint torque in real time.

- Musk distinguished scripted demonstrations from genuine AI that can handle unfamiliar situations.

- Mass production remains the goal, but the initial ramp will be slow. A dedicated humanoid-parts supply chain is also needed.

- Musk said China’s restrictions on motor-magnet exports delayed Optimus development by 2–3 months last year.

- Tesla intends to secure U.S. production of critical components against future supply disruptions.

7. Robotaxi: Expansion and Safety

- Robotaxi’s monthly growth is rapid despite its seemingly slow rollout, Musk said. Preventing injuries and fatalities takes priority.

- Tesla checks risks such as small animals at night, unusual intersections, and railroad crossings before entering new cities.

- It may initially use geofencing and deploy improvements after testing.

- A single Robotaxi accident could trigger global headlines and regulatory shutdowns, prompting cautious expansion.

The Florida Highwaymen were a collective of 26 African-American landscape painters who created a unique movement starting in Fort Pierce, Florida, during the late 1950s. Emerging during the Jim Crow era, these self-taught artists faced systemic exclusion from traditional galleries and museums. Instead of letting those barriers stop them, they developed a brilliant, rapid-painting technique and famously sold their fresh oil paintings right out of the trunks of their cars along Florida's highways.
Today, their work is recognized as a vital chapter in American art history, with pieces housed in prestigious institutions like the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture.

Vivid Natural Landscapes
The Highwaymen prioritized capturing the raw, untouched beauty of the Florida coast and backcountry. Their work famously highlights the state's dramatic ecosystems, emphasizing changing light and open skies.

text:
A white MP arrested a Black Navy officer for wearing his own uniform. The officer was Ensign Sam Gravely, twenty-three, from Richmond, Virginia, sitting in a Miami club with sailors from his ship in August 1945. The MP had never seen a Black naval officer before, so he took the uniform for a fake. Gravely answered him with one sentence straight out of Navy custom, and the night got much worse from there.

The MP told Gravely that the Shore Patrol chief waiting outside wanted to see him. Gravely stayed in his chair and answered, "If the Chief wants to see me, tell him to come here."

A chief petty officer is enlisted, and in the Navy the enlisted man walks over to the officer, never the other way around.

The MP pulled him up out of his chair. The sailors around them were plainly upset, and Gravely called out to them, "Take it easy." Then he added, "This is only a mistake."

Word spread across the room that the ensign was being taken in, and his own sailors closed in around the MP. The patrol radioed for help, and two more Shore Patrol trucks pulled up.

The new patrolmen found Gravely still trying to calm his men down and explain the mistake. They forced a number of the crew into the trucks, and Gravely rode to headquarters in the chief's vehicle.

Those sailors had known their new officer for about three months.

It was not the first door that had closed on Gravely. In 1940 the Army turned him away over a heart murmur, an excuse the naval historian Paul Stillwell calls phony.

The Navy had its own closed door. Until June 1, 1942, a Black man could enlist only as a messman, cooking and serving meals for officers.

That spring the Navy announced the change, and in September 1942 Gravely left Virginia Union University to enlist in the Naval Reserve.

In 1943, a white officer pushed him to apply for V-12. It was a Navy program that sent sailors to college on the way to an officer's commission. Gravely was accepted.

On October 1, 1943, he reported to the University of Southern California and was given five white roommates. The next morning he was called to the office and told he had been transferred. His gear went into a truck, and he went across town to UCLA.

The only reason he could think of, he said later, was that Black students like Jackie Robinson mostly went to UCLA.

At UCLA his room was picked for him too. In his own words, he was "assigned to the basement, with other rooms available all over that building."

He marched and trained beside his classmates, and he said there was no off-duty contact with any of them, not even on weekends. So he watched himself: "I watched my decorum, I watched everything."

On December 14, 1944, Gravely was commissioned an ensign. That came eight months after the Golden Thirteen, the Navy's first Black officers, were commissioned in March 1944.

Stillwell writes that Gravely was proud he had entered officer training before they did.

His first orders still sent him to Great Lakes, Illinois, to train Black recruits while most of his class headed for the war. "I was let down," he said. Six weeks later, by his own account, he was on his way to sea.

The ship was PC-1264, a submarine chaser the Navy had crewed as an experiment. Her officers were white, and most of her enlisted men were Black, put aboard to measure what Black sailors could do.

In the spring of 1945 Gravely became her first Black officer. A training stop that summer is what put him in that club.

At Shore Patrol headquarters that night, the duty officer apologized to Gravely once the mistake was explained. That detail comes from the ship's captain, Lieutenant Eric Purdon, in his 1972 book about the ship.

The next morning, the naval district's command wanted Purdon to court-martial the ensign. The charge they had in mind was "conduct unbecoming an officer and a gentleman."

The same Navy said sorry at night and asked for a trial in the morning.

Purdon refused. Navy regulations, he pointed out, did not let a district commander order a ship's captain to charge one of his own officers.

The sailors who had closed in around the MP faced charges of their own. The list ran from refusing Shore Patrol orders to interfering with the patrol to drunkenness. The captain kept his crew aboard ship, out of the patrol's reach, until they sailed for Key West a few days later.

One biographical account places the next rejection at Key West, in 1945. Alma Clark, the schoolteacher he would soon marry, later described the message his captain received: "He was to be informed that he could not come to the officer's clubs."

"I think it hurt him and embarrassed him in front of the others," she said. The Navy's own history office says that when an officers' club shut him out, he spent the time on Navy correspondence courses.

Nobody needed to let him into a correspondence course.

The war ended that August, and the ship was decommissioned in February 1946 with Gravely as her second in command. On February 12 he married Alma, whom he had courted with a letter every day until she said yes.

Back home, he finished his history degree at Virginia Union in 1948. He took a job as a railway postal clerk, sorting mail in moving train cars. He had planned to teach and coach, he told Ebony.

In 1949 the Navy invited a few Black officers back for one year, to help recruit Black sailors. Gravely was one of them, and when the Korean War broke out in 1950, he stayed on active duty for thirty more years.

As a recruiter, he felt he did not have enough sea time to describe Navy life honestly, so he asked for a ship. Before the Navy placed a Black officer aboard a ship, its personnel bureau first asked the ship's command whether it would accept him.

A white officer got orders, and Gravely got a question sent ahead of him.

The battleship Iowa said yes, and Gravely served aboard her as radio officer during the Korean War. On a cruiser a few years later, he was in a port bar in the western Pacific when he heard snickering behind him.

His roommate explained that the men were testing one of the old racist myths meant to paint Black people as less than human.

On his next ship, Gravely overheard a visiting commodore tell his captain, "I notice you have a colored lieutenant commander on board." The captain answered, in a sincere tone, "What color is he?"

By 1959 Gravely wanted destroyers, the Navy's small, fast fighting ships. Nearly fifteen years after his commission, he had never served on one, and the personnel bureau answered his request with orders for shore duty.

He wrote again with his captain's endorsement and got into a do-it-yourself training plan. He went from destroyer to destroyer asking to be taken aboard as a trainee, and not every ship made him welcome. He shadowed their executive officers and worked his way through every department aboard.

In January 1960, a destroyer that needed a new second in command gave him twenty-four hours to report. The next morning his wife drove him to the pier.

When the ship went into a San Francisco shipyard for a long overhaul, the Navy made him her temporary captain on February 15, 1961. No Black man had commanded a U.S. Navy ship since Robert Smalls, a civilian who held command during the Civil War.

A ship in the yard is still a ship, and for eight months this one was his.

Near the end of the overhaul, an assignment officer told him he was getting a ship of his own. It was a radar picket vessel based at Pearl Harbor. His reaction, in his own words: "I was so happy I'm not sure I heard anything else he said after that, because I was really, really overjoyed."

A few years later, working on communications at the Pentagon, he flew often on test runs of an airborne command post. A fellow officer told him to apply for flight pay, and he did, expecting the Navy to say no.

The Navy said no to the flight pay. It offered him command of a full destroyer.

He asked for a little extra money and got the thing he had been chasing since 1959.

In 1966 he took that destroyer to Vietnam, firing her guns at targets ashore and standing by to rescue downed pilots from the carriers. He was the first Black officer to lead a U.S. Navy ship into combat. Stillwell writes that Gravely loved being on the bridge during high-speed maneuvers.

He made captain in 1967, and in 1970 he took command of the guided-missile frigate Jouett.

In the spring of 1971, the Jouett stopped at Pearl Harbor on her way home from a deployment off Vietnam. Gravely went ashore to meet his commodore, and as he walked back toward the ship, the loudspeaker came on.

When a ship's commanding officer returns, the Navy rings a set number of bells over the speakers and announces the ship's name. A captain rates four bells, and a rear admiral rates six.

Gravely counted six, then heard "Jouett arriving."

He figured somebody had made a mistake. When he stepped aboard, his executive officer met him: "Congratulations, admiral. You made it. You made it."

He had just been selected as the first Black admiral in the history of the U.S. Navy. His sleeve still said captain, and his own ship had already rung him aboard as something more.

In 1976 he took command of an entire fleet, based in Hawaii, as a three-star vice admiral. He retired in 1980, thirty-eight years after he enlisted.

Gravely died on October 22, 2004, after a stroke, and was buried at Arlington National Cemetery.

In 2009 his widow christened a new destroyer named for him. "I'm so happy with the type of ship they chose because he loved destroyers," she said. About fifty years after the Navy answered his first destroyer request with shore duty, it put his name on one.

In the accounts of the Miami night that I could find, the charges against his sailors are listed and their names are not. Years later, Gravely explained why he had watched himself so closely at UCLA.

"I felt that I couldn't screw it up for the other people who might come along." In that club in Miami, some of those other people had already stood up for him.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter. If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/AeER0VXKqi
Every coffee helps me keep creating.

text:
So, an interesting article by @dex_eve and some counter points by @krakek1 regarding the operational employment of mobile missiles.

FWIW I’d offer the following:

1) you really can’t underestimate the degree the issue in the pic below (from Decker’s piece) is true. Well credentialed people with deep experience in strategic studies (heck, almost any field*) will be fundamentally ignorant of tech / policy details that are immediately adjacent their specialty. And they won’t even know it. Take everything with massive spoonfuls of salt.

2) I find Decker’s points interesting but ultimately less persuasive, not least because of issues raised by Krakek. There’s a lot of heavy lifting based on things like PLARF needing pre-surveyed launch sites (as an aside if you have one of those, why would you still need to program in the location? Surely one of the very points of such a spot is you know where it is to a nicety), the US having those all mapped out (hope none of them are able to be disguised!), and Washington being able to hit them all after successfully identifying the “fire all missiles” signal… the last part in particular is something I’m pretty sure Beijing would keep close to its chest.

* An old boss of mine was a PhD physicist who used to work on particle colliders. I asked him at one point how tight the coupling was between his practical work and the theoretical physicists - how quickly did the feedback cycle work? He rolled his eyes and said “We don’t talk to those nerds”. 

Reality is a fractal - and my goodness the left hand barely knows the right even exists half the time.

text:
Donald Trump’s new diesel deal with Vladimir Putin may offer temporary relief to energy markets, but it risks rewarding the very war Washington claims to oppose. The timing, and the message it sends to Ukraine, are deeply troubling.

The economic motivation is understandable. Rising fuel prices affect households, agriculture, transport and global trade. Yet Washington has now eased sanctions on Russian diesel, potentially restoring revenue to Moscow while its invasion of Ukraine continues. Energy analysts remain sceptical that the additional supplies will deliver meaningful, sustained price reductions. Strategically, it is difficult to see how relieving economic pressure on Russia, without securing reciprocal concessions, strengthens Ukraine’s negotiating position or brings lasting peace any closer.

What I find particularly troubling is the contradiction between Trump’s repeated ambitions for the Nobel Peace Prize and the consequences of his diplomacy. Peace cannot simply be measured by the number of agreements announced or the economic opportunities they create. It must also be judged by whom those agreements benefit, what principles they compromise, and whether they genuinely discourage further aggression. I regard this as a betrayal of Ukraine, with questionable economic rewards and potentially serious strategic consequences. A peace agreement that strengthens the aggressor while weakening the victim is hardly a convincing achievement.
